title: Care Guide & Patient Rights
subtitle: Practical guidance for medication access, legal rights, and daily flare management

susSection.title: How to Access Free / Subsidized IBD Medications
susSection.desc: Public healthcare systems and specialized programs provide comprehensive treatment for Ulcerative Colitis through clinical protocols.
susSection.step1: Specialized Medication Request Form filled and signed by your Gastroenterologist.
susSection.step2: Valid medical prescription with active ingredient name (e.g. Mesalamine 800mg or 1200mg) issued within 30-90 days.
susSection.step3: Detailed Medical Report containing clinical history, ICD-10 K51 (Ulcerative Colitis), and dosage rationale.
susSection.step4: Colonoscopy and Biopsy (histopathology) report confirming IBD diagnosis.
susSection.step5: Copies of personal documents: ID card, social security / health card, and recent proof of address.
susSection.medsList: Mesalamine (oral tablets, enemas, and suppositories), Sulfasalazine, Azathioprine, and Biologics / Small Molecules (Infliximab, Vedolizumab, Ustekinumab, Tofacitinib, etc.).
susSection.tip: 💡 Pro Tip: Renew your documentation every 3 to 6 months according to your local healthcare jurisdiction to prevent treatment interruptions.

compoundingSection.title: Savings with Certified Compounding Pharmacies
compoundingSection.desc: For topical formulations (mesalamine suppositories and retention enemas), licensed compounding pharmacies offer identical formulations with major cost savings.
compoundingSection.benefit1Desc: Compounded 500mg or 1g suppositories and 3g or 4g enemas cost substantially less than commercial brand-name counterparts.
compoundingSection.benefit2Desc: Ask your gastroenterologist to prescribe 'Compounded mesalamine suppositories/enemas' with the exact dosage and volume.
compoundingSection.benefit3Desc: Always select pharmacies with good manufacturing practices and rigorous raw material testing.

rightsSection.title: Your Legal Rights & Patient Protections
rightsSection.desc: Understand legal protections and accessibility rights for Inflammatory Bowel Disease patients.
rightsSection.right1Desc: Many jurisdictions have passed Restroom Access Acts mandating immediate access to employee restrooms in commercial venues for individuals with IBD.
rightsSection.right2Desc: Medical certificates and recognized IBD association cards (like CCFA or regional groups) serve as proof for priority seating and restroom access.
rightsSection.right3Desc: Patients during active flares qualify for priority customer service and workplace accommodations.
rightsSection.right4Desc: Severe or refractory cases may qualify for temporary medical leave or disability benefits under labor regulations.

flareCareSection.title: Practical Tips for Flare Management
flareCareSection.desc: Essential complementary measures to protect your bowel and soothe discomfort.
flareCareSection.care1Desc: With frequent loose stools, drink oral rehydration solutions, coconut water, or diluted electrolyte drinks in small sips to prevent dehydration and potassium loss.
flareCareSection.care2Desc: Avoid dry toilet paper. Use warm water bidets or handheld showers with neutral soap, and pat dry gently. Zinc oxide barrier creams protect against painful irritation.
flareCareSection.care3Desc: During active inflammation, favor easily digestible cooked foods (white rice, boiled potatoes, baked poultry, bananas). Avoid insoluble fiber, seeds, deep-fried foods, dairy, and excess caffeine.
flareCareSection.care4Desc: NSAIDs like ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac erode mucosal lining and can trigger severe bleeding or precipitate a severe flare.

doctorPrepSection.title: Preparing for Your Gastroenterology Visit
doctorPrepSection.desc: Get the most out of your consultation by bringing structured, objective data.
doctorPrepSection.prep1Desc: Export your 30 to 90-day summary from the History tab with frequency trends, blood tracking, and pain metrics.
doctorPrepSection.q1: 1. 'Is my mesalamine dosage optimized for mucosal healing and long-term remission?'
doctorPrepSection.q2: 2. 'Should we order a Fecal Calprotectin test to assess endoscopic mucosal healing?'
doctorPrepSection.q3: 3. 'Do I need to update non-live vaccinations before starting immunosuppressants or biologics?'
doctorPrepSection.q4: 4. 'What routine blood panels (CBC, ferritin, CRP, Vitamin D/B12) should we monitor?'
doctorPrepSection.prep3Desc: Always report any fever, nocturnal awakenings to defecate, or escalating severe abdominal pain.
